decisions.quote: A second issue concerned the age of acquisition of cardinal knowledge. Wynn (1992) claimed that children become CP-knowers around 3 ½ year-old (42 months) and reported an effect of age suggesting that younger children exhibit lower level of cardinal knowledge (one-, two-and three-knowers) than older children. A similar correlation between age and cardinal knowledge was indeed observed in Study 1. However, convergent observations from Study 1 and 2 indicates that cardinal knowledge were far from achieving maturity at the age of 3 ½ years.
decisions.reason: The paper states no single overarching replication verdict that overrides its specific comparisons to Wynn (1992). Across the tested claims, the authors explicitly report agreement with several original findings (overall correlation between age and cardinal knowledge level in Study 1, sequential acquisition of small number words, large inter-individual variability in age and developmental time span, and greater use of counting for large than small number words among large-number knowers) alongside explicit disagreement with others (children learned large number words 4-7 sequentially rather than generalizing all-at-once after 3 or 4, achieved full cardinal knowledge much later than 3.5 years, and succeeded at large numbers even with a grabbing strategy). Per the codebook, conflicting comparisons across tested claims yield 'mixed'.

decisions.quote: The present work focused on the GaN from Wynn's (1990Wynn's ( , 1992) ) studies with no intention to test the replicability of results coming from the other tasks (i.e., the Point-to-x task or the colour control task were not administered).
decisions.reason: Omitted target. The authors explicitly frame their work as a conceptual replication of the Give-a-Number (GaN) observations from both Wynn (1990) and Wynn (1992), and in Study 1 they directly re-test Wynn's (1990) counter vs. grabber strategy predictions (line 30) as well as the all-at-once generalization assumption attributed to Wynn (1990, 1992) (line 28), finding mixed support (confirming that large-number knowers count more frequently for large than small numbers, but finding sequential acquisition of large number words and no difference between terminal-counters and terminal-grabbers in reaching large-number knowledge).
